ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Tissue fixation preserves cellular architecture for microscopy by halting autolysis and putrefaction. Proper fixation is essential for accurate histopathologic diagnosis, especially when ischemic time is prolonged.

sections.p: Tissue fixation is the chemical preservation of specimens to maintain morphology and prevent enzymatic degradation and bacterial decay before microscopic analysis.
b: Uses aldehyde solutions (most commonly 10% neutral buffered formalin)

sections.p: Inadequate fixation results from delayed immersion, insufficient fixative volume, or improper temperature, leading to autolysis and artefacts.
b: Long ischemic time (>30 min for most tissues) is the common cause of poor fixation
Cold fixation can slow enzyme activity but may cause precipitation

sections.p: Poorly fixed tissue shows loss of nuclear detail, cytoplasmic vacuolisation, and artefactual staining, which can mimic disease.
b: Soft, mushy consistency
Discolouration or uneven staining on slides

sections.p: Assess fixation quality by gross inspection and microscopic review of control sections.

t.b: Is the tissue firm and uniformly pale? Soft, gelatinous tissue suggests inadequate fixation.

t.a: H&E slide of a control tissue
t.b: Does nuclear chromatin appear crisp? Faint nuclei indicate under‑fixation.

sections.p: Incorrect fixation can lead to misdiagnosis, delayed treatment, and repeat biopsies, increasing cost and patient anxiety.
b: Misinterpretation of malignancy grade
False negative for infectious organisms

sections.p: Ensure prompt immersion of fresh tissue in adequate volume of 10% neutral buffered formalin (20 × tissue volume) at room temperature; if unavailable, use alcohol‑based fixatives.
b: Limit ischemic time: aim <30 min for most organs, <1 h for bone
Maintain pH 7.0–7.4 to prevent artefacts
If formalin unavailable, use 70% ethanol as an alternative

sections.p: Document fixation time and fixative type on the pathology request form; audit specimen quality regularly to identify workflow gaps.
b: Standard operating procedure for specimen handling
Training of staff on rapid transport

sections.p: Autolysis (natural self‑digestion) and putrefaction (bacterial decay) are processes prevented by fixation, not fixation itself.
b: Autolysis occurs before fixation; putrefaction can continue if fixative is insufficient

sections.p: Over‑fixation (excess time >24 h) can mask antigenicity, leading to false‑negative immunohistochemistry, while under‑fixation may cause poor staining.
b: Immunostains may be weak or absent after prolonged fixation
Morphologic detail may be lost with inadequate fixation

faq.q: Why is formalin the fixative of choice?
faq.a: Formalin cross‑links proteins, preserving structure while allowing routine staining and most immunohistochemical tests.

faq.q: What is the acceptable ischemic time for a biopsy?
faq.a: Ideally less than 30 minutes; up to 1 hour is acceptable for most soft tissues, longer for bone.

faq.q: Can I use saline instead of formalin?
faq.a: No; saline does not stop enzymatic degradation and will lead to autolysis and artefacts.

exam: Explain how ischemic time influences tissue fixation quality and downstream diagnosis.
